design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis and dose–response meta-regression of case–control, nested case–control and cohort studies of alcohol intake and 23 cancer sites. 572 unique papers (704 site-specific papers; published 1956–2012) with 486,538 cancer cases. Each study's intake categories were converted to grams of ethanol per day (one drink = 12.5 g), assigned their midpoint and grouped as light (midpoint up to 12.5 g/day), moderate (above 12.5 and up to 50 g/day) or heavy (above 50 g/day) drinking, and compared with the study's reference group of nondrinkers, or nondrinkers and occasional drinkers combined (24.1% of studies). Pooling by DerSimonian–Laird random effects; nonlinear dose–response by two-term fractional-polynomial random-effects meta-regression; subgroup analyses by design, sex and world region. No protocol registration and no assessment of primary-study quality or publication bias.
can_establish: The average association reported in 572 observational studies published before September 2012 between light, moderate and heavy drinking and the risk of each of 23 cancers, relative to nondrinkers or occasional drinkers, and how far these associations differ by study design, sex and world region.
cannot_establish: That alcohol causes any of these cancers (the conclusion's causal verbs rest on IARC's classification, not on this analysis); that the small light-drinking associations are free of confounding by smoking, of under-reporting and of former drinkers in the reference group (none is assessed study by study, and about half the contributing estimates were unadjusted); absolute risks (none are reported); whether the pooled estimates are inflated by publication bias (not assessed here); or the effect of drinking pattern and beverage type (not analysed).

sample.recruitment: Literature search in MEDLINE, ISI Web of Science (Science Citation Index Expanded) and EMBASE for epidemiological studies published online before September 2012, plus reference lists of relevant studies, reviews and meta-analyses; English only; search terms in Supplementary Material S1 (not read) (Materials and methods › Search strategy). Figure 1 (flowchart, read on the rendered page): 31,473 non-unique records; 29,786 excluded on title or abstract; 1,687 full texts retrieved plus 210 from reference lists; 1,193 excluded as not meeting the inclusion criteria (no breakdown by reason); 704 site-specific papers, 572 unique (56 papers reported on more than one site). The primary studies are hospital- and population-based case–control series and cohorts: 41.3% from North America, 32.2% Europe, 17.7% Asia, 8.9% other or mixed areas (Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: case–control, cohort or nested case–control studies published as original articles, reporting an OR, RR or HR (or data to compute one) for at least two levels of intake against nondrinkers and/or occasional drinkers, with a standard error or CI (or data to compute one); cancer sites with five or more papers. Excluded: abstracts, letters, reviews and meta-analyses; studies of one beverage type only, because nondrinkers of that beverage might drink others. For duplicate publications the most recent or complete was kept, and a pooled analysis was preferred to its constituent study (Materials and methods › Inclusion criteria; Data abstraction, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Study level (Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1): 409 case–control (71.5%) and 163 cohort (28.5%) papers; 541 (94.6%) reported incidence and 31 (5.4%) mortality; 219 (38.3%) gave estimates for men, 256 (44.8%) for women and 179 (31.3%) for both sexes together (sex-specific papers counted twice); 297 (51.9%) reported adjusted estimates; 138 (24.1%) included occasional drinkers in the reference category. Largest sites: female breast 118 papers (117,317 cases in drinking categories, 48,433 in the reference category), colorectum 66, oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 54, oral cavity and pharynx 52; smallest: small intestine and cervix, 5 papers each. Participants' ages are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; not reported for the primary studies.
sample.selection_effects: English only, no grey literature or registries, and a search ending in September 2012 for a paper published online in November 2014. Eligibility for each site was judged by a single author (Data abstraction, 1st paragraph). Case–control studies dominate (409 of 572) and gave stronger associations than cohorts at several sites (oral cavity and pharynx, heterogeneity P=0.007; heavy drinking and liver cancer 2.79 in case–control vs 1.12 in cohort studies; larynx 2.81 vs 1.12; Table 2), which points to recall or control-selection effects in the case–control literature. Many contributing estimates were not adjusted for the main site-specific confounders: adjusted estimates were reported by 41 of 118 breast, 32 of 54 oesophageal squamous cell, 21 of 41 laryngeal and 14 of 36 liver cancer papers (Table 1).

exposure.measurement: As in each primary study (self-reported current or lifetime intake by questionnaire or interview; methods are not described study by study in the main text). The reviewers converted all units to g/day (0.8 g per ml, 28 g per ounce, 12.5 g per drink), assigned each category its midpoint (open upper category: 1.2 times its lower bound), classed categories as light, moderate or heavy by midpoint, and combined several estimates falling in one class within a study with Hamling's method (Materials and methods › Data abstraction, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Average volume only. Light = midpoint up to 12.5 g/day (up to about one 12.5-g drink a day); moderate = above 12.5 and up to 50 g/day (about one to four drinks); heavy = above 50 g/day (more than four drinks). Drinking pattern (such as heavy drinking occasions) and beverage type could not be analysed (Discussion, 10th paragraph). The fitted dose–response curves (Figure 3) are plotted over 0–100 g/day for most sites and 0–50 g/day for melanoma, cervix, endometrium, ovary and thyroid; no numeric curve parameters are printed.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco, the main confounder for upper aerodigestive, lung and other cancers, is handled only through whatever adjustment each primary study made (main confounders by site listed in Supplementary Material S2, not read); about half the pooled estimates are unadjusted. The authors discuss residual confounding by smoking for lung and stomach cancer and cite their own earlier meta-analysis finding no association between alcohol and lung cancer in never-smokers (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Other drugs are not considered.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Former drinkers may sit in the nondrinker reference group of primary studies; the review did not record or separate them (Discussion, 10th paragraph).

comparison.controls: Each study's lowest category: nondrinkers, or nondrinkers and occasional drinkers combined in 138 of 572 studies (24.1%). Whether nondrinkers were lifetime abstainers or included former drinkers was not recorded (Materials and methods › Data abstraction, 2nd paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. Adjusted estimates were used when available; otherwise the reviewers computed crude RRs from the raw data (Materials and methods › Statistical methods, 1st paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: By site: smoking, diet, obesity, diabetes, hepatitis B and C infection, reproductive and hormonal factors, socio-economic position and, in East Asian populations, ALDH2 genotype. Which were controlled varies by study and is listed only in Supplementary Material S2 (not read). The authors name under-reporting by drinkers, former drinkers in the reference group, and quitting because of early symptoms (lymphomas) as sources of misclassification.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Smoking in the reference groups is not reported at review level; other drug use is not considered.

outcomes.instruments: Incident cancer (541 studies) or cancer death (31 studies) by site, as defined in each primary study: oral cavity and pharynx; oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma; oesophageal adenocarcinoma and gastric cardia; stomach; small intestine; colorectum; liver; gallbladder; pancreas; larynx; lung; melanoma; female breast; cervix; endometrium; ovary; prostate; bladder; kidney; thyroid; brain; Hodgkin's lymphoma; non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: No quality or risk-of-bias assessment of the primary studies. Only adjustment status and the inclusion of occasional drinkers in the reference group were recorded, and both were used in sensitivity analyses.
outcomes.operationalization: Relative risk of each site-specific cancer for light, moderate and heavy drinking against the reference group; odds ratios, risk ratios and rate ratios were treated as equivalent because cancer is rare (Materials and methods › Statistical methods, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 64 counts the pooled category estimates in Figure 2 (23 sites by 3 intake categories, with heavy drinking not evaluable for 5 sites). The paper also reports 23 fitted dose–response curves, three subgroup tables (design, sex, area) with a heterogeneity test per site, and a publication-year analysis whose data are not shown.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Eligibility was judged by one author per site, with doubts resolved by consensus among all investigators; duplicate data extraction is not described.

analysis.covariates: None at review level: adjusted estimates were taken as reported (main site-specific confounders listed in Supplementary Material S2, not read), otherwise crude estimates were computed from raw data and pooled with them. Sensitivity analyses restricted to adjusted estimates, and excluding studies with occasional drinkers in the reference group, are reported as not materially changing the results (Supplementary Material S3, not read); the discussion gives only the pancreatic result (about a 20% increase with fully adjusted estimates).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration reported. MOOSE is cited only in the limitations paragraph.
analysis.selective_reporting: The main text and Figure 2 give each site's total number of studies but not the number behind each intake category. Sensitivity-analysis results are only in Supplementary Material S3, and the publication-year analysis is 'data not shown'. Two statistically significant inverse associations at light drinking that appear in Figure 2, lung cancer 0.84 (0.79–0.88) and oesophageal adenocarcinoma with gastric cardia 0.86 (0.76–0.98), are not mentioned in the text, and two significant subgroup heterogeneity tests are not discussed (ovary by design, P=0.007, Table 2; lung by area, P=0.045, Table 4).
analysis.power: Not addressed. Six sites rest on 5 to 9 studies (small intestine, cervix, brain, gallbladder, Hodgkin's lymphoma, thyroid), and subgroup analyses were limited to sites with more than 10 studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Higher risk with drinking for cancers of the oral cavity and pharynx (heavy drinking RR 5.13), oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (4.95), larynx (2.65), gallbladder (2.64), liver (2.07), female breast (1.61), colorectum (1.44), stomach (1.21), pancreas (1.19) and lung (1.15), compared with nondrinkers or occasional drinkers. At light drinking (up to 12.5 g/day) the associations were small and statistically significant only for oral cavity and pharynx (1.13, 1.00–1.26), oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (1.26), female breast (1.04, 1.01–1.07) and prostate (1.04). Inverse associations were found for kidney, thyroid and both lymphomas, and, at light drinking only, for lung cancer and oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Heterogeneity was high for many estimates (I² up to 91%), case–control studies gave stronger associations than cohorts at several sites, and about half of the contributing estimates were unadjusted.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the final paragraph state that alcohol “increases risk of cancer” of six sites (oral cavity and pharynx, oesophagus, colorectum, liver, larynx, female breast). Gaps: (1) the causal verb comes from IARC's classification, cited in the introduction; this pooling of observational associations, with no appraisal of the primary studies, cannot by itself show causation; (2) the abstract's conclusion names the oesophagus without qualification, whereas the association was confined to squamous cell carcinoma (adenocarcinoma: no positive association, and 0.86, 0.76–0.98, at light drinking); (3) the heavy-drinking breast estimate quoted in the abstract (1.61) rests on 11 of the 118 breast studies (Table 2), and only 41 of the 118 reported adjusted estimates (Table 1); (4) the discussion reads the inverse kidney association as support for a protective effect of moderate drinking, while it explains the inverse lymphoma association by misclassification, and the final paragraph then lists kidney among cancers with no association; (5) the statement that oral, oesophageal and breast cancer were associated with drinking even at low doses sits beside the authors' concession that under-reporting by drinkers may partly or largely explain the light-drinking associations (Discussion, 9th and 10th paragraphs). Against this, the discussion names residual confounding by smoking for lung and stomach cancer and treats the pancreas, prostate and melanoma findings cautiously.

timeline.event: IARC Working Group lists alcohol drinking as carcinogenic for the oral cavity and pharynx, oesophagus, liver and larynx (as summarised in this paper's introduction).
Bagnardi et al., earlier meta-analysis by the same group based on 235 studies, which this paper updates.
IARC monograph volume 100E (cited in this paper as IARC Working Group, 2010) adds colorectum and female breast to the sites for which alcohol is carcinogenic.

Bagnardi et al., the group's meta-analysis of light drinking and cancer, which this paper says it updates and corroborates; it estimated about 5000 oral and pharyngeal, 24,000 oesophageal squamous cell and 5000 breast cancer deaths attributable to light drinking worldwide in 2004 (as cited in this paper's discussion).

Heinen et al., a Dutch cohort of 120,852 people, found no inverse association between alcohol and lymphoid neoplasms, against this review's inverse lymphoma estimates (as cited in this paper's discussion).

Rumgay et al. estimate the global cancer burden attributable to alcohol with relative risks from the WCRF Continuous Update Project rather than this review, using IARC's list of causal sites and leaving out the inverse kidney association (card sc_rumgay_2021).

replication.where_it_stands: The most comprehensive site-by-site dose–response meta-analysis of alcohol and cancer up to 2012, and a common source of site-specific relative risks by intake category. Its positive associations for the oral cavity and pharynx, oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, larynx, colorectum, liver and female breast agree with IARC's causal classification, which the paper cites rather than tests. Its light-drinking estimates (RR 1.04 to 1.26 at three sites) are small enough for confounding, under-reporting and former drinkers in the reference group to matter, and the review neither appraised study quality nor examined publication bias. Claims should cite it for the direction and approximate size of each site's association, stating the reference group (nondrinkers, sometimes with occasional drinkers), the 12.5-g drink and the category bounds (light up to 12.5 g/day, moderate up to 50 g/day, heavy above 50 g/day).

funding.funder: Italian Association for Cancer Research (AIRC), Project No. 10258 (My First AIRC Grant), and the Italian Foundation for Cancer Research (FIRC); FT supported by a FIRC fellowship; MR and CG supported by Fondazione Umberto Veronesi (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of Milan-Bicocca, the European Institute of Oncology, the Mario Negri Institute, the University of Milan, the Besta Neurological Institute, IARC (Lyon), the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, the American Cancer Society, Emory University, the Karolinska Institute, the Istituto Nazionale Tumori and Tehran University of Medical Sciences. The same group wrote most of the earlier site-specific meta-analyses this review updates, and it refers questions such as publication bias to those papers. No industry funding is stated. Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For the low-intake associations: a pooled individual-participant analysis of prospective cohorts with lifetime abstainers as the reference, repeated intake measures, full adjustment for smoking with results in never-smokers, and estimates by site and histology reported as absolute risks; and genetic analyses using variants in alcohol-metabolising genes (ALDH2, ADH1B) in populations where they are common, by cancer site.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (participants of human case–control and cohort studies), exposure (alcohol intake by g/day category), comparator (nondrinkers and/or occasional drinkers), outcomes (23 site-specific cancers, incidence or mortality) and eligible designs are stated (Materials and methods › Inclusion criteria).
No protocol or registration is reported.

Case–control, nested case–control and cohort studies were included without a stated reason. The choice is self-evident for an exposure that cannot be randomized, but the item asks for the explanation.

Three databases and reference lists, but English only without a justification, no grey literature or registry search, search terms only in a supplement, and a search ending more than two years before online publication (September 2012; November 2014). Under AMSTAR 2 as the project applies it (decision 21), an unjustified language limit gives 'no'.
The reports for each site were reviewed for eligibility by one author, with doubts resolved by consensus among all investigators (Data abstraction, 1st paragraph).
Duplicate extraction, or checking by a second reviewer, is not described.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 reports 1,193 full-text papers excluded as not meeting the inclusion criteria, without reasons by category and without a list. The supplements as the paper describes them (S1 search terms, S2 confounders, S3 sensitivity analyses, S4 list of included studies, S5 study-specific estimates) include no list of excluded studies.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: the main text describes the included studies only in aggregate by site (Table 1: design, outcome, area, sex, adjustment, reference group). Study-level information is in Supplementary Materials S4 (list of studies) and S5 (study-specific estimates), which were not read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias or quality assessment of the primary studies; only adjustment status and the presence of occasional drinkers in the reference group were recorded.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: The techniques are appropriate in themselves: random-effects pooling (DerSimonian–Laird), Hamling's method for correlated estimates within a study, and a dose–response meta-regression that allows for within-study correlation. But the headline estimates combine adjusted estimates with crude RRs computed from raw data for about half the studies (297 of 572 reported adjusted estimates), with no reason given beyond availability; the adjusted-only analysis is a sensitivity analysis reported only in Supplementary Material S3. The methods also call the heterogeneity small while I² reaches 91% (Figure 2), and no prediction intervals are given. A close call, judged not met because crude and adjusted estimates are mixed in the main results.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses restricted to adjusted estimates and excluding studies with occasional drinkers in the reference group, and subgroup analyses by design, examine two main sources of bias (results reported as not materially changed; Supplementary Material S3, not read). Former drinkers in the reference group were not examined.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The discussion weighs residual confounding by smoking (lung, stomach) and poor diet, misclassification from under-reporting and from former drinkers among nondrinkers, and reverse causation for the lymphomas (Discussion, 5th, 7th and 10th paragraphs). The abstract's causal conclusions are not qualified by these points; judged met on balance.

I² is reported for every pooled estimate (Figure 2; Tables 2–4); heterogeneity was investigated by design, sex and area with F tests and by publication year, and high heterogeneity is acknowledged as the first limitation.
Not investigated in this paper; the authors refer to their earlier site-specific meta-analyses (Discussion, 10th paragraph).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and a no-conflict statement are given (Acknowledgments).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 8 can be judged only from Supplementary Materials S4–S5, which were not read; it is not a critical item and cannot change the rating. Six critical items are not met (2 protocol, 4 search, 7 excluded studies, 9 appraisal of primary studies, 11 statistical methods, a close call, and 15 publication bias), with 13 met, so AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. This rates how far the pooled numbers can be taken as unbiased summaries, not the paper's usefulness. In practice: (a) the light-drinking RRs of 1.04 to 1.26 lie in a range that confounding (about half the estimates unadjusted), under-reporting and former drinkers in the reference group could produce or mask; (b) small-study and publication effects were not examined; (c) with I² up to 91%, a single pooled RR describes no particular population. The large heavy-drinking associations for upper aerodigestive cancers are consistent in direction across designs, sexes and regions (Tables 2–4) and are the most robust results. The paper may be cited for site-specific associations by intake category, with these caveats, but not as evidence of causation or of risk at very low intake on its own.

key_findings.finding: 572 unique papers (704 site-specific; 409 case–control, 163 cohort) published 1956–2012 contributed 486,538 cancer cases across 23 sites; 541 reported incidence and 31 mortality; 297 (51.9%) reported adjusted estimates and 138 (24.1%) included occasional drinkers in the reference category.

Exposure definitions used for every pooled estimate: intake in grams of ethanol per day with one drink = 12.5 g; categories by midpoint as light (up to 12.5 g/day), moderate (above 12.5 and up to 50 g/day) and heavy (above 50 g/day); reference group nondrinkers, combined with occasional drinkers in 24.1% of studies; former drinkers not separated.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Data abstraction, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Oral cavity and pharynx (52 studies), RR vs nondrinkers or occasional drinkers: light 1.13 (95% CI 1.00–1.26), moderate 1.83 (1.62–2.07), heavy 5.13 (4.31–6.10); I² 26%, 72% and 77%. Oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (54 studies): 1.26 (1.06–1.50), 2.23 (1.87–2.65), 4.95 (3.86–6.34); I² 68%, 85% and 91%. Larynx (41 studies): light 0.87 (0.68–1.11), moderate 1.44 (1.25–1.66), heavy 2.65 (2.19–3.19).
key_findings.note: I² values are printed in Figure 2 (read on the rendered page), not in the text.

key_findings.finding: Female breast cancer (118 studies), RR vs nondrinkers or occasional drinkers: light 1.04 (1.01–1.07), moderate 1.23 (1.19–1.28), heavy 1.61 (1.33–1.94); I² 63%, 54% and 10%.
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic from Table 2: the heavy-drinking estimate rests on 11 studies (6 cohort, 5 case–control), the moderate on 95 and the light on 115. Only 41 of the 118 breast studies reported adjusted estimates (Table 1).

key_findings.finding: Colorectum (66 studies): light 0.99 (0.95–1.04), moderate 1.17 (1.11–1.24), heavy 1.44 (1.25–1.65). Liver (36 studies): light 1.00 (0.85–1.18), moderate 1.08 (0.97–1.20), heavy 2.07 (1.66–2.58). Heavy drinking was also associated with stomach (1.21, 1.07–1.36; 39 studies), pancreas (1.19, 1.11–1.28; 39), lung (1.15, 1.02–1.30; 34) and gallbladder cancer (2.64, 1.62–4.30; 8 studies). All vs nondrinkers or occasional drinkers.

Prostate (43 studies): light 1.04 (1.01–1.08), moderate 1.06 (1.01–1.11), heavy 1.09 (0.98–1.21). Melanoma (14 studies): light 1.11 (0.97–1.27), moderate 1.20 (1.03–1.41), heavy not evaluable. No significant positive association for oesophageal adenocarcinoma and gastric cardia, small intestine, cervix, endometrium, ovary, bladder or brain.

Inverse associations vs nondrinkers or occasional drinkers: Hodgkin's lymphoma 0.73 (0.59–0.89), 0.73 (0.60–0.87) and 0.63 (0.41–0.97) for light, moderate and heavy drinking (9 studies); non-Hodgkin's lymphoma 0.88 (0.80–0.97), 0.87 (0.81–0.95) and 0.75 (0.64–0.88) (24 studies); kidney light 0.92 (0.86–0.99) and moderate 0.79 (0.72–0.86) (17 studies); thyroid light 0.81 (0.74–0.88) and moderate 0.81 (0.71–0.94) (9 studies). Figure 2 also shows inverse associations at light drinking for lung cancer, 0.84 (0.79–0.88), and oesophageal adenocarcinoma with gastric cardia, 0.86 (0.76–0.98), which the text does not mention.

By design (Table 2): case–control studies gave stronger associations than cohort studies for oral cavity and pharynx (heavy drinking 5.34, 4.46–6.39, 35 studies vs 3.13, 1.59–6.19, 3 studies; heterogeneity P=0.007). Heavy drinking and liver cancer: 2.79 (2.00–3.87) in 24 case–control vs 1.12 (1.02–1.23) in 7 cohort studies; larynx 2.81 (2.33–3.39) vs 1.12 (0.75–1.67), 3 cohorts (heterogeneity tests not significant). Light drinking and liver cancer in cohorts: 0.85 (0.74–0.97). Melanoma was associated with drinking only in the 2 cohort studies (light 1.25, moderate 1.27).

By sex (Table 3): the colorectal association was stronger in men (light 1.05, moderate 1.21, heavy 1.53, 1.30–1.80) than in women (0.95, 1.07, and 1.24, 0.68–2.25, from 4 studies; heterogeneity P=0.010); no significant colorectal association in women.

By region (Table 4): light drinking was significantly associated with oral cavity and pharynx (1.33, 1.06–1.68; 7 studies) and oesophageal squamous cell cancer (1.54, 1.18–2.00; 11 studies) only in Asian studies; melanoma (light 1.32, moderate 1.47) and prostate cancer (1.05, 1.09, 1.20) only in North American studies; the non-Hodgkin's lymphoma association differed by region (P=0.013), with no association in European studies.

Restricting to adjusted estimates, or excluding studies with occasional drinkers in the reference category, did not materially change the results; the prostate association emerged more clearly in both sensitivity analyses. For pancreatic cancer, fully adjusted estimates alone still gave a significant increase of about 20% for heavy drinking.
key_findings.note: Sensitivity-analysis estimates are in Supplementary Material S3, not read; only the pancreatic figure is given in the main text.

key_findings.finding: Dose–response meta-regression (Figure 3): risk rose steeply with intake for oral cavity and pharynx and oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma; increased risk for stomach and liver cancer was observed at about 25 g/day (two drinks); risk of lymphomas decreased linearly with dose; lower doses were inversely associated with kidney and thyroid cancer.
key_findings.note: Figure 3 shows curves only (log RR axis; 0–100 g/day for most sites, 0–50 g/day for melanoma, cervix, endometrium, ovary and thyroid); no values were extracted from it.

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: high heterogeneity for some cancers; drinking pattern and beverage type not analysed; under-reporting by drinkers may partly or largely explain the light-drinking associations; former drinkers in the nondrinker category may dilute risks; heterogeneous exposure measurement; publication bias and control type deferred to the group's earlier site-specific meta-analyses.

The authors suggest the inverse lymphoma association may partly reflect misclassification, because early symptoms may lead people to stop or reduce drinking, and they cite a European cohort of 120,852 people that found no inverse association.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says the meta-analysis supports a protective effect of moderate drinking on renal cell cancer (8th paragraph), but the concluding paragraph lists kidney among cancers with no apparent association with alcohol, while the results report significant inverse associations (light 0.92, 0.86–0.99; moderate 0.79, 0.72–0.86).
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper gives two incompatible readings of its kidney result; neither can be cited as the authors' conclusion without the other, and the protective reading is not tested against the misclassification explanation the authors apply to lymphomas.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says alcohol was not significantly associated with oesophageal adenocarcinoma and gastric cardia, but Figure 2 gives a light-drinking RR of 0.86 (0.76–0.98), whose interval excludes 1; the light-drinking lung cancer RR of 0.84 (0.79–0.88) is also absent from the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two significant inverse associations at light drinking appear only in the figure; they matter for judging the light-drinking category as a whole (for example confounding or reference-group effects that lower RRs at low intake).

reporting_issues.issue: The methods say random-effects models were used to allow for heterogeneity that is described as small, while Figure 2 shows I² up to 91% and the limitations call heterogeneity high for some cancers.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Materials and methods › Statistical methods, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2; Discussion, 10th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Internal inconsistency; the pooled estimates for oesophageal squamous cell, oral, laryngeal, liver and lung cancer at heavy drinking (I² 73% to 91%) summarise widely varying studies.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1, stomach row: 33 studies of incidence plus 5 of mortality make 38, not the 39 studies listed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor counting error; one stomach study is unaccounted for in the outcome columns.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 2 and the text label each site with its total number of studies (for example female breast, 118), but the pooled estimate for each intake category uses a subset; the heavy-drinking breast estimate of 1.61, quoted in the abstract, rests on 11 studies (editors' sum of the cohort and case–control counts in Table 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers will overrate the evidence behind the heavy-drinking estimates; study counts per category are available only for sites with more than 10 studies, through Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: Two significant subgroup heterogeneity tests are not mentioned in the text: ovary by study design (P=0.007, Table 2) and lung cancer by world region (P=0.045, Table 4; heavy drinking 1.26 in North American, 0.96 in European and 0.92 in Asian studies).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor selective reporting; the lung cancer association at heavy drinking may be confined to North American studies.
